Appendix A Featured topological domains and lifting maps

We adopt the featured-domain and lifting formalism of TopoBench (Telyatnikov et al., 2025a), restricting the presentation to the objects used in this study. The input to every lifting is a featured graph, and the output is a featured graph, hypergraph, simplicial complex, or cell complex.

A.1 Featured topological domains

Definition 1 (Featured graph).

A featured graph is a tuple

𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ,F𝒱,Fℰ),F𝒱:𝒱→ℝd𝒱,Fℰ:ℰ→ℝdℰ.\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},F_{\mathcal{V}},F_{\mathcal{E}}),\qquad F_{\mathcal{V}}:\mathcal{V}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathcal{V}}},\qquad F_{\mathcal{E}}:\mathcal{E}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathcal{E}}}.

Here, (𝒱,ℰ)(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) specifies the underlying graph, with 𝒱\mathcal{V} being the set of nodes and ℰ\mathcal{E} the set of edges. While F𝒱F_{\mathcal{V}} and FℰF_{\mathcal{E}} assign the node and edge features, respectively. We omit FℰF_{\mathcal{E}} when the edge features are not available.

Topological domains.

A topological domain is a discrete representation of a system in terms of its constituent elements and the relations among them. Beyond pairwise graph edges, these relations may connect several nodes or organize elements through containment, incidence, or boundary relations. The term therefore provides a common language for graphs and their higher-order generalizations (Hajij et al., 2023; Papillon et al., 2024; Telyatnikov et al., 2025a).

Higher-order domains.

We consider three families of higher-order domains. Hypergraphs represent set-type relations by allowing a hyperedge to connect any number of nodes, without imposing a hierarchy among hyperedges. Simplicial complexes add a strict part-whole hierarchy in which every simplex contains all of its lower-dimensional faces. Cell complexes retain a boundary-based hierarchy but admit non-simplicial cells, including polygonal faces that can represent graph cycles directly (Hajij et al., 2023; Papillon et al., 2024; Telyatnikov et al., 2025a).

Definition 2 (Hypergraph).

Let 𝒫⁡(𝒱)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{V}) denote the power set of a non-empty node set 𝒱\mathcal{V}. A hypergraph on 𝒱\mathcal{V} is a pair H=(𝒱,ℰH)H=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}_{H}), where ℰH⊆𝒫⁡(𝒱)∖{∅}\mathcal{E}_{H}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{V})\setminus\{\emptyset\}.

Definition 3 (Simplicial complex).

A simplicial complex on a non-empty node set 𝒱\mathcal{V} is a pair S=(𝒱,𝒳)S=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{X}), where 𝒳⊆𝒫⁡(𝒱)∖{∅}\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{V})\setminus\{\emptyset\} and

σ∈𝒳,∅≠τ⊆σ⟹τ∈𝒳.\sigma\in\mathcal{X},\quad\emptyset\neq\tau\subseteq\sigma\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\tau\in\mathcal{X}.

The elements of 𝒳\mathcal{X} are called simplices.

Definition 4 (Cell complex).

A regular cell complex is a topological space SS partitioned into cells {xα}α∈PS\{x_{\alpha}\}_{\alpha\in P_{S}}, where PSP_{S} is an index set, such that:

  1. 1.

    S=⋃α∈PSint⁡(xα)S=\bigcup_{\alpha\in P_{S}}\operatorname{int}(x_{\alpha}).

  2. 2.

    for every α∈PS\alpha\in P_{S}, the interior of xαx_{\alpha} is homeomorphic to ℝnα\mathbb{R}^{n_{\alpha}} for some nα∈ℤ≥0n_{\alpha}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}, and nαn_{\alpha} is the dimension of xαx_{\alpha}.

  3. 3.

    the boundary of each cell is a union of finitely many cells of strictly lower dimension.

The experimental liftings instantiate these domains using node neighbourhoods as hyperedges, cliques as simplicial cells, and graph cycles as cellular 2-cells, as detailed in Appendix A.2.1.

Definition 5 (Featured topological domain).

Let 𝒯=(𝒳,F)\mathcal{T}=(\mathcal{X},F), where 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a topological domain, and

F={Fr}r≥0,Fr:𝒳r→ℝdrF=\{F_{r}\}_{r\geq 0},\qquad F_{r}:\mathcal{X}_{r}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d_{r}}

assigns feature vectors to its rank-rr elements. For hypergraphs the feature maps instead distinguish nodes and hyperedges.

A.2 Lifting maps

Definition 6 (Lifting between featured topological domains).

Let 𝒯src=(𝒳src,Fsrc)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{src}}=(\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{src}},F_{\mathrm{src}}) be the featured source domain and 𝒯tgt=(𝒳tgt,Ftgt)\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{tgt}}=(\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{tgt}},F_{\mathrm{tgt}}) the featured target domain. A lifting ℒ:𝒯src→𝒯tgt\mathcal{L}:\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{src}}\rightarrow\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{tgt}} consists of a structural map ℒS\mathcal{L}_{S} and a feature map ℒF\mathcal{L}_{F}:

𝒳tgt=ℒS​(𝒳src,Fsrc),Ftgt=ℒF​(𝒳src,Fsrc),ℒ⁡(𝒯src)=𝒯tgt.\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{tgt}}=\mathcal{L}_{S}(\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{src}},F_{\mathrm{src}}),\qquad F_{\mathrm{tgt}}=\mathcal{L}_{F}(\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{src}},F_{\mathrm{src}}),\qquad\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{src}})=\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{tgt}}. (1)

The structural map constructs the elements and incidence relations of 𝒳tgt\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{tgt}}, while the feature map transfers or constructs their features FtgtF_{\mathrm{tgt}}.

This definition follows the lifting formalism of TopoBench (Telyatnikov et al., 2025a). In our experiments, 𝒯src\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{src}} is a featured graph and 𝒯tgt\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{tgt}} is the representation required by the model. For example, the clique-complex lifting constructs simplicial cells from graph cliques and assigns features to the resulting elements. All structural liftings used in this study derive the target domain from graph connectivity.

For B⊆𝒱B\subseteq\mathcal{V}, the featured graph provided to a mini-batch lifting is

𝒢B=(B,ℰB,F𝒱|B,Fℰ|ℰB),ℰB={(u,v)∈ℰ:u,v∈B},\mathcal{G}_{B}=\left(B,\mathcal{E}_{B},\left.F_{\mathcal{V}}\right|_{B},\left.F_{\mathcal{E}}\right|_{\mathcal{E}_{B}}\right),\qquad\mathcal{E}_{B}=\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}:u,v\in B\},

with the edge-feature term omitted when unavailable. During mini-batch training and inference, the workflow constructs ℒ⁡(𝒢B)\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{G}_{B}) directly without first materializing ℒ⁡(𝒢)\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{G}).

A.2.1 Lifting maps used in the experiments

The experiments instantiate each lifting on a featured graph 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ,F𝒱,Fℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},F_{\mathcal{V}},F_{\mathcal{E}}). We first specify its structural component ℒS\mathcal{L}_{S}. The identity lifting preserves the input features, whereas the higher-order liftings use a common feature map that assigns features to the constructed elements. Each construction applies to either the full graph or an induced mini-batch graph, with 𝒢B\mathcal{G}_{B} substituted for 𝒢\mathcal{G}. The lifting-specific scale parameters and their experimental values are stated below.

Identity graph lifting.

The identity lifting preserves the graph and its features,

ℒid​(𝒢)=𝒢.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{id}}(\mathcal{G})=\mathcal{G}.

We use it with GCN.

kk-hop neighbourhood hypergraph lifting.

The kk-hop lifting assigns a hyperedge to the closed kk-hop neighbourhood of each node (Telyatnikov et al., 2025a). For an integer k≥1k\geq 1 and a node v∈𝒱v\in\mathcal{V}, define

N𝒢(k)​[v]={u∈𝒱:dist𝒢⁡(u,v)≤k},N_{\mathcal{G}}^{(k)}[v]=\{u\in\mathcal{V}:\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal{G}}(u,v)\leq k\},

where dist𝒢\operatorname{dist}_{\mathcal{G}} denotes shortest-path distance in 𝒢\mathcal{G}. The resulting node-indexed hyperedge family and structural lifting are

ℰH(k)=(ev)v∈𝒱,ev=N𝒢(k)​[v],ℒS,khypergraph​(𝒢)=(𝒱,ℰH(k)).\mathcal{E}_{H}^{(k)}=\bigl(e_{v}\bigr)_{v\in\mathcal{V}},\qquad e_{v}=N_{\mathcal{G}}^{(k)}[v],\qquad\mathcal{L}_{S,k}^{\mathrm{hypergraph}}(\mathcal{G})=\left(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}_{H}^{(k)}\right).

The center-node index is retained, so the implementation creates exactly one incidence-matrix column per node even when two indexed hyperedges have identical memberships. The parameter kk determines the graph radius represented by each hyperedge. We set k=1k=1 and use this lifting with EDHNN and UniGNN.

Cycle-basis cell lifting.

Cycle-based cellular liftings attach 2-cells along selected graph cycles (Bodnar et al., 2021; Telyatnikov et al., 2025a). Let ℬ⁡(𝒢)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G}) denote a fundamental cycle basis obtained using Paton’s algorithm (Paton, 1969). For a maximum cycle length ℓmax\ell_{\max}, we retain

ℬ≤ℓmax​(𝒢)={c∈ℬ⁡(𝒢):|c|≤ℓmax}.\mathcal{B}_{\leq\ell_{\max}}(\mathcal{G})=\{c\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G}):|c|\leq\ell_{\max}\}.

Attaching one 2-cell along each retained cycle gives

ℒS,ℓmaxcell​(𝒢)=(𝒞0,𝒞1,𝒞2),𝒞0=𝒱,𝒞1=ℰ,𝒞2=ℬ≤ℓmax​(𝒢).\mathcal{L}_{S,\ell_{\max}}^{\mathrm{cell}}(\mathcal{G})=(\mathcal{C}_{0},\mathcal{C}_{1},\mathcal{C}_{2}),\qquad\mathcal{C}_{0}=\mathcal{V},\qquad\mathcal{C}_{1}=\mathcal{E},\qquad\mathcal{C}_{2}=\mathcal{B}_{\leq\ell_{\max}}(\mathcal{G}).

We set ℓmax=9\ell_{\max}=9 and use this lifting with CWN and TopoTune.

Clique-complex lifting.

The clique-complex lifting maps every clique of size r+1r+1 to an rr-simplex (Bodnar et al., 2021; Telyatnikov et al., 2025a). For a maximum simplex dimension dmaxd_{\max}, define the truncated clique complex

Cl≤dmax(𝒢)={∅≠σ⊆𝒱:|σ|≤dmax+1,(u,v)∈ℰfor all distinct u,v∈σ}.\mathrm{Cl}_{\leq d_{\max}}(\mathcal{G})=\left\{\emptyset\neq\sigma\subseteq\mathcal{V}:|\sigma|\leq d_{\max}+1,(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}\ \text{for all distinct }u,v\in\sigma\right\}.

The corresponding structural lifting is

ℒS,dmaxsimplicial​(𝒢)=(𝒱,Cl≤dmax​(𝒢)).\mathcal{L}_{S,d_{\max}}^{\mathrm{simplicial}}(\mathcal{G})=\left(\mathcal{V},\mathrm{Cl}_{\leq d_{\max}}(\mathcal{G})\right).

We set dmax=2d_{\max}=2, yielding nodes, edges, and filled triangles. We use this lifting with SCN and SCCNN.

Feature lifting.

The preceding maps specify the structural component ℒS\mathcal{L}_{S} of each lifting. In the experiments, the common feature component ℒF\mathcal{L}_{F} retains existing features and constructs missing higher-rank features by summing over incident lower-rank elements (Telyatnikov et al., 2025a). For a ranked domain, let 𝐁r,r+1\mathbf{B}_{r,r+1} be the incidence matrix between rank-rr and rank-(r+1)(r+1) elements. The feature assignment from 𝐗r\mathbf{X}_{r} to 𝐗r+1\mathbf{X}_{r+1} is

𝐗r+1=|𝐁r,r+1|𝖳​𝐗r.\mathbf{X}_{r+1}=\left|\mathbf{B}_{r,r+1}\right|^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}_{r}.

The absolute value removes orientation signs, and the operation is applied successively across ranks. For a hypergraph with node-hyperedge incidence matrix 𝐇\mathbf{H}, the corresponding assignment is 𝐗H=|𝐇|𝖳​𝐗0\mathbf{X}_{H}=|\mathbf{H}|^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{X}_{0}, where 𝐗0\mathbf{X}_{0} is the input node-feature matrix. Each new element therefore receives the sum of the features on its incident source elements. The feature assignment does not alter the structure produced by ℒS\mathcal{L}_{S}.

Appendix B Practical scalability of graph-supported TDL: bottlenecks and solution paths

B.1 Pipeline view of graph-supported TDL scalability

The scalability of graph-supported TDL depends on the entire computational pipeline, not only on the TNN architecture. The input graph must first be lifted by identifying higher-order structures and constructing their feature matrices and connectivity operators. In the evaluated implementation, the constructed representation is held in CPU memory and transferred to the GPU as needed for training or inference. A bottleneck at any one of these stages can make an otherwise efficient architecture impractical.

Where these costs occur depends on the execution regime. Full-domain execution constructs the topology and lifts features once during preprocessing, then reuses the complete lifted representation throughout training and evaluation. Cluster-TNN instead partitions the graph during preprocessing and reconstructs and lifts individual induced graph mini-batches during training and inference. This shift trades full-domain storage for repeated local construction and therefore changes preprocessing, execution time, and memory jointly. Both regimes use the same parameterized lifting procedure and structural restrictions. Applying that procedure to induced subgraphs, however, need not produce the restriction of the full-domain lift.

We use the notation introduced in Appendix A. For a lifting ℒ=(ℒS,ℒF)\mathcal{L}=(\mathcal{L}_{S},\mathcal{L}_{F}), the stored representation depends on the number of generated elements |𝒳r||\mathcal{X}_{r}|, the number of entries in its incidence or neighbourhood operators, and the feature width drd_{r} at each rank. The structural counts in Table 3 determine the number of feature rows. The feature widths convert those row counts into the storage estimates in Table 4. Table 5 distinguishes models that request different operators from the same lifted domain.

B.2 Representation growth: from structure to storage

Structural expansion and feature storage are related but distinct. We first explain how liftings create higher-order structures and represent their connectivity (Sec. B.2.1). We then compare the structural characteristics of the benchmarks and their lifted domains (Sec. B.2.2). Finally, we combine these structural counts with feature dimensions to estimate feature-matrix storage (Sec. B.2.3).

B.2.1 Lifting-specific mechanisms of structural expansion

Different liftings can produce very different numbers of higher-order structures from the same graph. The connectivity information also varies, including node memberships in hyperedges and the edges forming cell boundaries. We illustrate these sources of growth using the neighbourhood-hypergraph, cycle-based cellular, and clique-complex liftings used in our experiments, which are TopoBench’s default graph mappings to the corresponding domains.

Neighbourhood-hypergraph lifting.

For the evaluated k=1k=1 neighbourhood-hypergraph lifting, each node defines one indexed hyperedge containing its closed one-hop neighbourhood. The number of hyperedges is therefore exactly |𝒱||\mathcal{V}| for every dataset and provides no additional distinction beyond the node count. Connectivity nevertheless determines the incidence size. Across all neighbourhood hyperedges, the lifting stores |𝒱|+2​|ℰ||\mathcal{V}|+2|\mathcal{E}| node-hyperedge memberships, corresponding to an average hyperedge size of 1+2​|ℰ|/|𝒱|1+2|\mathcal{E}|/|\mathcal{V}|.

Cycle-based cellular lifting.

The cycle-based cellular lifting first computes a fundamental cycle basis and retains cycles of length at most ℓmax=9\ell_{\max}=9, attaching one cellular 2-cell along every retained cycle. Each retained cycle contributes one 2-cell and one nonzero entry in the edge-cell incidence matrix for each edge on its boundary. Its storage requirements therefore depend on both the number and lengths of the retained cycles. The retained cycle basis can also change when the lifting is recomputed on an induced subgraph, as discussed in Appendix C.13.22 2 The evaluated implementation computes the complete cycle basis before discarding cycles longer than ℓmax\ell_{\max}. The length restriction therefore bounds the retained cell complex, but not necessarily the time or temporary memory required to construct the basis.

Clique-complex lifting.

The clique-complex lifting fills every graph triangle with a simplicial 2-cell. Triangle-rich graphs can therefore produce far more 2-cells than input nodes or edges. In the stored representation, each generated 2-cell contributes one feature-vector row and three nonzero entries to the edge-cell incidence matrix, one for each boundary edge.

B.2.2 Benchmark scale regimes and coverage

Table 3 reports the numbers of input nodes and edges, together with the numbers of 2-cells generated by the cellular and simplicial liftings.33 3 For the evaluated k=1k=1 neighbourhood-hypergraph lifting, the hyperedge count is |𝒱||\mathcal{V}| and the node-hyperedge membership count is |𝒱|+2​|ℰ||\mathcal{V}|+2|\mathcal{E}|. Both follow from the input-graph columns and are omitted from the table. Mean node degree, calculated as 2​|ℰ|/|𝒱|2|\mathcal{E}|/|\mathcal{V}|, describes how many neighbours an input node has on average. It distinguishes graphs with similar edge counts but substantially different node counts.

For each lifting, the Per node column divides the total number of generated 2-cells by the number of input nodes. This shows how large the generated 2-cell set is relative to the original node set. The absolute counts describe the size of the lifted domain, while these ratios allow us to compare structural expansion across graphs of different sizes. They are ratios of total counts, not counts of the cells incident to an average node.

Input and lifted scale regimes.

Questions, Amazon Ratings, and Cora Full have mean node degrees between 6.286.28 and 7.607.60. Coauthor Physics reaches 14.3814.38 and produces 13.5813.58 simplicial 2-cells per node, placing it between the smaller controlled benchmarks and the two scalability-oriented cases.

Reddit and OGBN Products expose complementary scalability regimes. OGBN Products contains approximately 10.5×10.5\times more nodes, yet the two graphs have comparable edge counts. Reddit consequently has a mean node degree of 491.99491.99, compared with 50.5250.52 for OGBN Products. The higher-order constructions also differ in their expansion. Reddit contains 174.20174.20 cellular and 35886.6735886.67 simplicial 2-cells per node, whereas OGBN Products contains 13.9813.98 and 253.60253.60, respectively. These datasets therefore contrast greater higher-order expansion per node with a substantially larger input node count at comparable edge counts.

Why the benchmarks are complementary.

The same progression gives the datasets complementary experimental roles. Questions, Amazon Ratings, and Cora Full support controlled comparisons between full-domain and Cluster-TNN partitioned execution because every evaluated lifting can be constructed on the complete graph. Coauthor Physics represents an intermediate case in which a moderate node count already produces substantially greater higher-order expansion. Reddit and OGBN Products extend the suite to graphs with tens of millions of edges and contrasting node counts. Together, these datasets support controlled comparisons with full-domain execution and allow us to examine how graph size, connectivity, and lifting-induced structural expansion affect computational cost.

The benchmarks also cover distinct application domains and relation semantics. Questions and Reddit represent online interactions, although Questions connects users through question-answer activity and Reddit connects posts through shared commenters (Platonov et al., 2023; Hamilton et al., 2017a). Cora Full and Coauthor Physics represent scientific-information networks through citation and coauthorship relations (Bojchevski and Günnemann, 2018; Shchur et al., 2019). Amazon Ratings and OGBN Products represent product co-purchasing networks at different scales (Platonov et al., 2023; Hu et al., 2020). Together, these datasets expose the pipeline to graph structures generated by different relational processes while keeping the downstream task fixed as node classification.

B.2.3 Static feature-matrix storage

Here, static feature-matrix storage denotes the persistent rank-wise input feature matrices of the full lifted domain. It excludes incidence tensors, derived operators, temporary construction objects, activations, gradients, and optimizer state.

Feature width provides a further source of variation across the benchmarks. Cora Full and Coauthor Physics have input widths of 8 7108\,710 and 8 4158\,415, respectively, compared with 602602 for Reddit and 100100 for OGBN Products. Their wider features increase storage per generated element, so a smaller graph need not have a proportionally smaller feature-storage requirement.

The memory required for the rank-wise feature matrices follows directly from the structural counts. At rank rr, the feature matrix contains |𝒳r||\mathcal{X}_{r}| rows and drd_{r} values per row. We assume single-precision floating-point storage (float32), which requires four bytes per value. Storing the feature matrices through rank two therefore requires

Mfeatures=4​(|𝒳0|​d0+|𝒳1|​d1+|𝒳2|​d2)​bytes.M_{\mathrm{features}}=4\left(|\mathcal{X}_{0}|d_{0}+|\mathcal{X}_{1}|d_{1}+|\mathcal{X}_{2}|d_{2}\right)\ \text{bytes}. (2)

For these estimates, each generated element receives a feature vector with the dataset’s input feature width, consistent with the feature assignment described in Appendix A.2.1. For cellular and simplicial domains, this gives d0=d1=d2d_{0}=d_{1}=d_{2} and Mfeatures=4​d0​∑r|𝒳r|M_{\mathrm{features}}=4d_{0}\sum_{r}|\mathcal{X}_{r}|. For hypergraphs, we count the node and hyperedge feature matrices. Table 4 uses the structural counts in Table 3. Other numerical precisions may be appropriate depending on the features and numerical requirements. For unchanged matrix dimensions, storage scales directly with the number of bytes per value. These estimates account only for input feature matrices, not total preprocessing or training memory.

For OGBN Products, substituting d0=d1=d2=100d_{0}=d_{1}=d_{2}=100 and the structural counts from Table 3 into Eq. (2) gives 39.414 GB for the cellular feature matrices and 274.156 GB for the simplicial feature matrices.

For Reddit, the cellular calculation is explicit:

Mfeaturescell\displaystyle M_{\mathrm{features}}^{\mathrm{cell}} =4×602×(232 965+57 307 946+40 582 059)\displaystyle=4\times 602\times\left(232\,965+57\,307\,946+40\,582\,059\right)
=236 280 111 760​bytes≈236.280​GB.\displaystyle=236\,280\,111\,760\ \text{bytes}\approx 236.280\ \text{GB}. (3)

Replacing the cycle-cell count with Reddit’s 8.368.36B simplicial 2-cells in the same calculation gives the 20.270 TB simplicial estimate reported in Table 4. Thus, before adding sparse incidence tensors or any neural-network state, the feature matrices alone can require hundreds of gigabytes for the cellular lifting and tens of terabytes for the simplicial lifting. This estimate results from storing a 602-dimensional float32 feature vector for every node, edge, and generated higher-order element.

B.3 Full-domain CPU preprocessing: construction time and memory

The analytical estimate above accounts only for persistent rank-wise feature matrices. The evaluated implementation stores incidence relations sparsely and constructs only the additional operators requested by a model.44 4 See the reproducibility statement for implementation and reproduction information. Cellular models may derive adjacency or Laplacian operators from cell incidences, while simplicial models may derive Laplacians from simplicial incidences. Full-domain preprocessing can therefore hold incidence matrices, derived operators, temporary construction objects, and implementation overhead in memory at the same time. We measure peak CPU memory as the largest resident-set size (RSS) sampled for the main Python process during full-domain preprocessing. It should be interpreted as the largest sampled resident-memory footprint of the main process, rather than as the size of any single tensor. Sampling may miss short-lived peaks and does not include memory held exclusively by child processes. Table 5 reports the available measurements for the evaluated dataset-lifting-model configurations.

For OGBN Products, the higher-order structures can be constructed, but retaining their complete feature matrices exceeds the available CPU RAM in the affected full-graph configurations. Even if this preprocessing bottleneck were overcome, full-graph training is expected to exceed the available GPU memory. We therefore report partitioned results with Cluster-TNN, while omitting incomplete full-graph preprocessing measurements from Table 5.

Reddit full-domain bottlenecks.

For Reddit, Eq. (3) predicts 236.280 GB for the cellular feature matrices alone, before accounting for incidence matrices, model-requested operators, and temporary allocations. Across five runs, CWN preprocessing takes 4684.8±304.84684.8\pm 304.8 s and reaches a peak CPU memory usage of 479.96±0.12479.96\pm 0.12 GB.

Storing the full Reddit simplicial input feature matrices at the original feature width in float32 would require an estimated 20.270 TB (Table 4).

B.4 Phase-specific memory during preprocessing and TNN execution

The following paired analyses focus on Questions, Amazon Ratings, and Cora Full, the three controlled benchmarks with complete full-graph and Cluster-TNN measurements across all seven evaluated models. Together, they provide 21 matched model-dataset comparisons. Each execution setting uses its independently selected hyperparameters, as reported in Appendix E. These comparisons therefore characterize the resource requirements and predictive performance of the tuned configurations.

Successfully constructing a lifted full domain does not imply that the complete representation can be processed by a TNN in one optimization step. A TNN layer may update several ranks and retain intermediate messages for backpropagation. For example, an edge representation can receive separate messages from incident nodes and 2-cells. These intermediate tensors add to the GPU memory required by the input features and connectivity operators.

Figure 5 places preprocessing CPU-memory peaks alongside training and evaluation GPU-memory peaks for all seven evaluated models, complementing the joint memory-runtime comparison in Figure 3.

For the depth-scaling experiment in Figure 4, peak reserved GPU memory is measured over five seeds, with each run lasting three epochs. This experiment uses 512512 hidden channels, K=64K=64, and q=8q=8.

Across the displayed comparisons, Cluster-TNN execution lowers peak GPU memory during both training and evaluation, whereas preprocessing CPU memory varies by configuration. These phase-specific measurements locate where memory pressure occurs. The next subsection reports elapsed time and peak CPU and GPU memory over a complete run.

B.5 End-to-end cost

End-to-end scalability has two distinct empirical dimensions: elapsed time across workflow phases and the peak CPU and GPU memory reached anywhere during a run. We report them separately because Cluster-TNN execution can reduce peak memory while increasing repeated lifting, validation, or inference time.

B.5.1 End-to-end runtime

An end-to-end comparison must account for when each method incurs its costs. Full-domain execution constructs the lifted domain once before training, whereas Cluster-TNN constructs the graph partition once and lifts mini-batches repeatedly. Table 6 reports preprocessing, training including validation passes, final validation and test inference, and total runtime for the 2121 matched model-dataset comparisons, together with partitioned-only results on Coauthor Physics, Reddit, and OGBN Products. Table 5 reports the separate full-domain preprocessing measurements.

For configuration ii, let t¯iFG\bar{t}_{i}^{\mathrm{FG}} and t¯iP\bar{t}_{i}^{\mathrm{P}} denote the mean total runtimes under full-graph and partitioned execution reported in Table 6. Its relative change is Δi=(t¯iP−t¯iFG)/t¯iFG×100%\Delta_{i}=(\bar{t}_{i}^{\mathrm{P}}-\bar{t}_{i}^{\mathrm{FG}})/\bar{t}_{i}^{\mathrm{FG}}\times 100\%, with negative values indicating reductions. We calculate changes in individual runtime components analogously. The reported means and medians give each configuration equal weight within the relevant subset.

The preprocessing component is shorter under Cluster-TNN partitioned execution in 1616 comparisons, longer in four, and unchanged in one. Among the 1616 decreases, the mean and median reductions are 53.9%53.9\% and 53.1%53.1\%. Among the four increases, the mean and median increases are 66.0%66.0\% and 36.7%36.7\%. These partitioned preprocessing measurements include the one-off graph-partitioning cost. Training time is lower in 1212 comparisons by 60.2%60.2\% on average (median 63.3%63.3\%) and higher in nine by 203.9%203.9\% on average (median 138.5%138.5\%). Mean total runtime is lower for all matched GCN and hypergraph configurations, higher for all cellular configurations, and lower for simplicial configurations only on Questions. This pattern describes the evaluated configurations rather than an intrinsic runtime ordering of the domains.

To complement these comparison-level summaries, Table 7 pools mean total runtimes within each subset. For a set of matched configurations ℐ\mathcal{I}, the pooled relative change is

Δpooled​(ℐ)=∑i∈ℐt¯iP−∑i∈ℐt¯iFG∑i∈ℐt¯iFG×100%.\Delta_{\mathrm{pooled}}(\mathcal{I})=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\bar{t}_{i}^{\mathrm{P}}-\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\bar{t}_{i}^{\mathrm{FG}}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\bar{t}_{i}^{\mathrm{FG}}}\times 100\%.

This aggregate weights each configuration’s relative change by its full-graph runtime. Across the matched benchmark suite, the additional runtime of slower configurations outweighs the savings of faster configurations. It describes the evaluated suite’s combined runtime rather than the change for a typical configuration.

CWN on Cora Full illustrates why training time and total runtime must be distinguished. Under partitioned execution, mean training time, including periodic validation, decreases from 909.6909.6 to 776.2776.2 seconds, a reduction of 14.7%14.7\%. However, final evaluation increases from 14.614.6 to 272.4272.4 seconds, resulting in a 12.4%12.4\% increase in total runtime. In this configuration, the additional evaluation cost outweighs the training-time reduction.

Across the 2121 matched comparisons, final evaluation is longer under partitioned execution in every case, with a median partitioned-to-full-graph time ratio of 11.75×11.75\times. These measurements include checkpoint validation and test inference, using ten-recombination ensemble mini-batch inference for Cluster-TNN. This measured difference includes both repeated evaluation and batch-construction costs. It is not an intrinsic lower bound for partitioned inference.

Validation caching convention.

In these experiments, we do not cache lifted validation batches. We reconstruct and lift each validation batch online. We include validation-batch construction costs in the training component for validation during fitting and in the final-evaluation component for checkpoint validation. Final evaluation includes checkpoint validation and test inference.

B.5.2 Run-wide peak memory

Unlike Table 5, which isolates full-domain preprocessing, Table 8 and 9 report peak CPU and GPU memory over the complete execution of each full-graph and Cluster-TNN run. CPU memory is the maximum sampled RSS of the main Python process, while GPU memory is the maximum CUDA memory allocated by the process.

Across the 21 matched full-graph and partitioned comparisons in Table 8, run-wide peak CPU memory is lower under partitioned execution in 15 comparisons by 14.8%14.8\% on average (median 2.4%2.4\%) and higher in six by 6.8%6.8\% on average (median 3.7%3.7\%). CPU memory therefore varies by configuration rather than exhibiting the uniform decrease observed for GPU memory. Peak GPU memory is lower in all 21 comparisons by 83.2%83.2\% on average (median 86.7%86.7\%).

Table 9 extends the measurements to Coauthor Physics, Reddit, and OGBN Products, reporting absolute memory requirements where matched full-graph results are unavailable. The larger-dataset results show that large input graphs can be processed with modest GPU memory requirements under Cluster-TNN execution. On Reddit, mean peak GPU memory ranges from 0.040.04 GB for UniGNN to 7.457.45 GB for SCCNN. On OGBN Products, TopoTune and SCN have mean peaks of 1.461.46 and 5.425.42 GB, respectively. Memory requirements therefore depend strongly on the sampled graph context and model configuration, rather than input graph size alone.

B.6 Structural exposure and statistical efficiency

Memory savings are only one consequence of batch-before-lift execution. Because each update is formed from an induced graph batch, the method also changes which full-graph structures can occur together and how often the model encounters them. We refer to this availability across cluster recombinations as structural exposure.

An epoch under Cluster-TNN visits all active training clusters once and groups them into mini-batches of at most qq clusters. Its number of optimization steps is therefore the number of active clusters divided into groups of size at most qq. The theory in Appendix C considers the simplified case in which all KK clusters are active and q|Kq\mid K, giving exactly M=K/qM=K/q steps. Increasing qq uses more memory per mini-batch but can expose more cross-cluster higher-order structures. Consequently, equal epoch counts need not represent equal update counts, wall-clock time, or structural information.

The recovery theory describes when structures and messages are available. It does not establish convergence to the model trained on the full lifted domain. We therefore assess statistical efficiency through validation trajectories, optimization steps, and test performance. The primary validation metric selects the checkpoint for each run. Test predictions from that checkpoint use full-graph inference for full-graph setting and ten-recombination ensemble inference for Cluster-TNN setting.

Table 10 and 11 summarize each validation trajectory by the checkpoint attaining the best primary validation metric. For each run, we associate this checkpoint with its completed optimizer-step count and its final test result.

Based on the reported means, partitioned training reaches the selected checkpoint in fewer epochs in 19 of 21 comparisons, but uses more optimizer updates in 20. Because a partitioned epoch contains multiple updates, epoch counts alone do not establish greater optimization efficiency. They should be interpreted alongside optimizer updates, elapsed time, and predictive performance.

B.7 Solution paths and practical guidance

The measurements above show a phase-specific trade-off rather than a uniform reduction in computational cost. Partitioned execution lowers peak GPU memory in all 21 direct comparisons, while preprocessing time, training time, and run-wide CPU memory change in both directions across configurations. Final evaluation is longer under the evaluated ten-recombination protocol, and statistical outcomes vary by dataset and model. A suitable remedy must therefore be matched to the stage that constitutes the binding bottleneck.

Alternative solution paths.

Different remedies address different stages of the workflow. Restricting neighbourhood radius, simplex dimension, or retained cycle length can reduce the number of retained higher-order elements or incidences, but may discard useful structure. For the evaluated neighbourhood lifting, reducing the radius changes membership volume rather than the fixed count of one indexed hyperedge per node. For the evaluated cycle lifting, the length cap filters retained cells after a complete cycle basis is computed, so it need not reduce basis-construction time or temporary memory. Reducing feature width or numerical precision lowers feature storage. Computing higher-order features when needed can avoid retaining their complete matrices, but introduces repeated computation and does not by itself remove the need to provide the required connectivity.

When full-domain construction exceeds CPU memory, batch-before-lift, distributed construction, or out-of-core processing address the construction stage in different ways. Distributed construction spreads work and allocations across workers, while out-of-core processing moves part of the representation to secondary storage. Neither reduces the representation itself. When the domain can be constructed but model execution exceeds GPU memory, sampling within the higher-order domain becomes a viable alternative. When repeated local lifting dominates runtime, caching a fixed set of lifted batches can reduce reconstruction work at the cost of storage and a fixed collection of cluster combinations.

Published lift-then-batch methods provide concrete examples in the hypergraph setting. Telyatnikov et al. (Telyatnikov et al., 2025b) sample hyperedges and then nodes within the sampled hyperedges, while FastHGNN (Lu and Ng, 2024) performs layer-wise node and hyperedge sampling. These methods reduce model-execution cost after a hypergraph is available, but do not address the cost of constructing a lifted domain from a source graph. They also do not directly specify how to sample simplicial or cellular domains while preserving the face or boundary relations used by those models.

Batch-before-lift: scope and trade-offs.

Batch-before-lift instead limits how much of the source graph is presented to the lifting and the TNN at one time. It is operationally applicable to graph-to-higher-order liftings that can be evaluated on induced subgraphs. This condition does not guarantee that locally lifted structures coincide with restrictions of the full-domain lift. For non-compatible liftings, local recomputation can alter the selected structures in addition to omitting structures whose supporting nodes do not appear together. Its principal costs are therefore repeated local lifting and reduced or altered structural exposure. The number of clusters grouped into a mini-batch controls part of this trade-off: larger batches can expose more cross-cluster structure, but require more CPU and GPU memory. Lift-then-batch methods address a complementary setting, particularly when data are observed natively as higher-order domains, but require sampling rules that preserve the relations used by the target hypergraph, simplicial, or cellular model. Standardized, intrinsically higher-order benchmark datasets remain comparatively scarce (Papamarkou et al., 2024; Rieck, 2026). Our implementation realizes batch-before-lift through TopoBench’s existing dataset, lifting, and model interfaces.

Reporting guidance.

At minimum, scalable graph-supported TDL studies should report lifting-induced structural growth, phase-wise time and peak memory with the device and measurement scope identified, end-to-end runtime, and predictive results. Where applicable, they should also report partition and mini-batch parameters, caching and inference protocols, the number of cluster recombinations, and optimizer updates. Together, these quantities distinguish whether a method reduces the representation itself, constructs it incrementally or on demand, limits only the model input, or trades repeated computation against storage. The realized memory savings and structural exposure depend on the dataset and lifting, as well as method-specific choices such as the partition, total number of clusters, mini-batch grouping, and number of recombinations. Appendix C next states the compatibility assumptions and formalizes the structural-exposure side of this trade-off.

Appendix C Structural reconstruction

This appendix analyzes which full-graph structures Cluster-TNN workflow recovers, how often it exposes them, and when their direct-incidence messages are available. The graph partition is fixed, and the only randomness comes from independently reshuffling its cluster indices at each epoch. Throughout the paper, KK denotes the total number of clusters in this partition. The implementation retains only clusters containing at least one target node from the current split (Sec. 3.1). For example, a cluster containing validation or test nodes but no training nodes is inactive for training. The number of active clusters can therefore be smaller than KK. The analysis below assumes that all KK partition clusters participate in recombination. For notational simplicity, we assume q|Kq\mid K, so every mini-batch contains exactly qq clusters. This removes a possible smaller remainder mini-batch without changing the qualitative conclusions. The following results state the compatibility assumptions required for structural recovery, repeated exposure, and direct-message availability.

The recovery analysis assumes compatibility with induced subgraphs, as formalized in Definition 7. This condition holds for the identity lifting, the evaluated kk-hop neighbourhood liftings, and the clique-complex lifting. It can fail for the cycle-basis lifting because restricting the graph can change the selected basis. The cycle-basis recovery probabilities therefore require stable basis membership. Appendix C.13 examines this condition empirically on Cora Full dataset.

C.1 Setup and notation

Because features do not affect structural recovery, let 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) denote the underlying undirected graph. Let

Π={P1,…,PK}\Pi=\{P_{1},\ldots,P_{K}\}

be the fixed partition of 𝒱\mathcal{V} into KK clusters considered in this analysis. We write [K]={1,…,K}[K]=\{1,\ldots,K\} and use q≤Kq\leq K clusters per mini-batch. Under the divisibility assumption above, each epoch contains M=K/qM=K/q mini-batches.

At each epoch t∈{1,…,T}t\in\{1,\ldots,T\}, we independently draw a uniformly random permutation of [K][K]. We divide the permutation into the mini-batch index sets

𝒵(t)={Z1(t),…,ZM(t)},Zi(t)⊆[K],|Zi(t)|=q.\mathcal{Z}^{(t)}=\{Z_{1}^{(t)},\ldots,Z_{M}^{(t)}\},\qquad Z_{i}^{(t)}\subseteq[K],\qquad|Z_{i}^{(t)}|=q.

For each mini-batch index set Zi(t)Z_{i}^{(t)}, we define the induced mini-batch graph

𝒢i(t)=(𝒱i(t),ℰi(t)),𝒱i(t)=⋃k∈Zi(t)Pk,ℰi(t)={(u,v)∈ℰ:u,v∈𝒱i(t)}.\mathcal{G}_{i}^{(t)}=\big(\mathcal{V}_{i}^{(t)},\mathcal{E}_{i}^{(t)}\big),\qquad\mathcal{V}_{i}^{(t)}=\!\!\bigcup_{k\in Z_{i}^{(t)}}\!\!P_{k},\qquad\mathcal{E}_{i}^{(t)}=\{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}:u,v\in\mathcal{V}_{i}^{(t)}\}.

Thus, 𝒢i(t)\mathcal{G}_{i}^{(t)} is the graph induced by the mini-batch node set B=𝒱i(t)B=\mathcal{V}_{i}^{(t)}.

Let ℒS\mathcal{L}_{S} be a deterministic structural lifting from graphs to a chosen topological domain. Let 𝒮\mathcal{S} denote the set of possible topological structures. For any graph 𝒢\mathcal{G}, we write Str⁡(ℒS​(𝒢))⊆𝒮\mathrm{Str}(\mathcal{L}_{S}(\mathcal{G}))\subseteq\mathcal{S} for the structures in the resulting lifted domain. The set observed in epoch tt is

S(t)=⋃i=1MStr⁡(ℒS​(𝒢i(t))).S^{(t)}=\bigcup_{i=1}^{M}\mathrm{Str}\left(\mathcal{L}_{S}\left(\mathcal{G}_{i}^{(t)}\right)\right)~. (4)

The cumulative observed set of structures after TT epochs is S^T=⋃t=1TS(t)\widehat{S}_{T}=\displaystyle\bigcup_{t=1}^{T}S^{(t)}.

The global structure set is S∗=Str⁡(ℒS​(𝒢))S^{\ast}=\mathrm{Str}\left(\mathcal{L}_{S}\left(\mathcal{G}\right)\right), obtained by lifting the full graph. We assume that 𝒢\mathcal{G}, and hence S∗S^{\ast}, is finite. Mini-batch lifting may also produce structures outside S∗S^{\ast}. We therefore define the observed global structures as

S^T∗=S^T∩S∗.\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}=\widehat{S}_{T}\cap S^{\ast}.

Thus, the recovery analysis only tracks global structures and ignores mini-batch-local artifacts.

For s∈S∗s\in S^{\ast}, given its vertex set 𝒱s⊆𝒱\mathcal{V}_{s}\subseteq\mathcal{V}, we define its partition-index support as

Is={i∈[K]:Pi∩𝒱s≠∅}I_{s}=\{i\in[K]:P_{i}\cap\mathcal{V}_{s}\neq\emptyset\}

and its cluster span cs=|Is|c_{s}=|I_{s}| as the number of clusters that ss intersects. Since every structure contains at least one vertex, we have cs≥1c_{s}\geq 1. A structure with cs=1c_{s}=1 is fully contained in one cluster.

Definition 7 (Lifting compatibility).

The lifting map is compatible with induced subgraphs if the following equivalence holds for every s∈S∗s\in S^{\ast} and every Zi(t)Z_{i}^{(t)}. The global structure ss appears in the lifted mini-batch exactly when that mini-batch contains all its supporting cluster indices:

s∈Str⁡(ℒS​(𝒢i(t)))⇔Is⊆Zi(t).s\in\mathrm{Str}\left(\mathcal{L}_{S}\left(\mathcal{G}_{i}^{(t)}\right)\right)\iff I_{s}\subseteq Z_{i}^{(t)}~.

C.2 Per-epoch recovery probability

We first compute the probability that a fixed global structure s∈S∗s\in S^{\ast} is recovered during one epoch. By Definition 7, all indices in IsI_{s} must occur in the same mini-batch. Thus, recovery depends on the cluster span cs=|Is|c_{s}=|I_{s}|. It is impossible when cs>qc_{s}>q and becomes a combinatorial co-occurrence event when cs≤qc_{s}\leq q.

Let

ps(t)=ℙ⁡(s∈S(t))p_{s}^{(t)}=\mathbb{P}\left(s\in S^{(t)}\right)

denote this per-epoch recovery probability. Since the reshuffling distribution is identical across epochs, ps(t)p_{s}^{(t)} does not depend on tt, and we write psp_{s}.

Lemma 1 (Per-epoch recovery probability).

For any global structure s∈S∗s\in S^{\ast},

ps={(q−1cs−1)(K−1cs−1),cs≤q,0,cs>q.\displaystyle p_{s}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\binom{q-1}{c_{s}-1}}{\binom{K-1}{c_{s}-1}},&c_{s}\leq q,\\[11.00008pt] 0,&c_{s}>q.\end{cases}
Proof.

If cs>qc_{s}>q, no mini-batch can contain all csc_{s} supporting cluster indices, so ps=0p_{s}=0. Now suppose cs≤qc_{s}\leq q. Fix k∈Isk\in I_{s}, and let Z(t)​(k)Z^{(t)}(k) be its unique mini-batch in epoch tt. Under a uniform shuffle, the other q−1q-1 members of Z(t)​(k)Z^{(t)}(k) form a uniformly random subset of [K]∖{k}[K]\setminus\{k\}. Recovery requires this subset to contain the fixed set Is∖{k}I_{s}\setminus\{k\}. Therefore,

ps=(K−csq−cs)(K−1q−1)=(q−1cs−1)(K−1cs−1).p_{s}=\frac{\binom{K-c_{s}}{q-c_{s}}}{\binom{K-1}{q-1}}=\frac{\binom{q-1}{c_{s}-1}}{\binom{K-1}{c_{s}-1}}~.

∎

Structures contained in one cluster are recovered every epoch. When q<Kq<K, the recovery probability decreases with cluster span, and structures with cs>qc_{s}>q remain unobservable.

C.3 Repeated structural exposure

Per-epoch recovery determines whether a structure is available during one epoch. To track repeated availability, for each s∈S∗s\in S^{\ast} we define the exposure indicator

Xs(t)=𝟏{s∈S(t)},X_{s}^{(t)}=\mathbf{1}\{s\in S^{(t)}\}~, (5)

where 𝟏​{⋅}\mathbf{1}\{\cdot\} denotes the indicator function, and the number of epochs in which ss has been observed by epoch TT,

Ns​(T)=∑t=1TXs(t).N_{s}(T)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}X_{s}^{(t)}~. (6)

The mini-batches partition the KK clusters in each epoch. A compatible global structure can therefore occur in at most one mini-batch per epoch. Thus, Ns​(T)N_{s}(T) counts both exposure epochs and the corresponding optimization steps containing ss.

Proposition 1 (Repeated structural exposure).

Under independent epoch reshuffling and lifting compatibility, for every fixed s∈S∗s\in S^{\ast},

Xs(t)​∼i.i.d.​Bernoulli⁡(ps),Ns​(T)∼Binomial⁡(T,ps).X_{s}^{(t)}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{s}),\qquad N_{s}(T)\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(T,p_{s}). (7)

Consequently,

𝔼⁡[Ns​(T)]=T​ps,Var⁡[Ns​(T)]=T​ps​(1−ps),\mathbb{E}[N_{s}(T)]=Tp_{s},\qquad\operatorname{Var}[N_{s}(T)]=Tp_{s}(1-p_{s}), (8)

and

Ns​(T)T⟶psalmost surely as ​T→∞.\frac{N_{s}(T)}{T}\longrightarrow p_{s}\qquad\text{almost surely as }T\to\infty. (9)
Proof.

By Lemma 1, each Xs(t)X_{s}^{(t)} is Bernoulli with success probability psp_{s}. It is a function of the permutation drawn in epoch tt. Independent and identically distributed epoch permutations therefore produce independent and identically distributed exposure indicators. Their sum is binomial, giving Eq. (7) and the moments in Eq. (8). Eq. (9) follows from the strong law of large numbers. ∎

Proposition 1 gives psp_{s} two interpretations. It is the one-epoch recovery probability and the asymptotic fraction of epochs containing ss. If cs=1c_{s}=1, then Ns​(T)=TN_{s}(T)=T almost surely. If cs>qc_{s}>q, then Ns​(T)=0N_{s}(T)=0 almost surely. When q<Kq<K, structures with 1<cs≤q1<c_{s}\leq q remain observable but occur less frequently than structures contained in one cluster.

Since every epoch contains M=K/qM=K/q optimization steps, Eq. (9) also gives the asymptotic fraction of all training steps in which ss is present:

Ns​(T)M​T⟶psMalmost surely as ​T→∞.\frac{N_{s}(T)}{MT}\longrightarrow\frac{p_{s}}{M}\qquad\text{almost surely as }T\to\infty. (10)

The distinction is important: psp_{s} is a per-epoch exposure probability, whereas ps/Mp_{s}/M is the corresponding frequency among optimization steps.

Remark 1 (Dependence between structures).

Proposition 1 concerns one fixed structure across epochs. Exposure indicators for different structures within an epoch are generally dependent because they share the same cluster grouping. None of the expectations below require independence between structures.

C.4 Cumulative recovery probability

Cumulative recovery records whether a global structure has been exposed at least once by epoch TT. For every s∈S∗s\in S^{\ast}, this event is equivalent to

{s∈S^T∗}={Ns(T)≥1}.\{s\in\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}\}=\{N_{s}(T)\geq 1\}.

By Proposition 1, the probability that ss remains unobserved after TT epochs is

ℙ⁡(s∉S^T∗)=ℙ⁡(Ns​(T)=0)=(1−ps)T.\mathbb{P}\left(s\notin\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}\right)=\mathbb{P}\left(N_{s}(T)=0\right)=(1-p_{s})^{T}.

Hence,

ℙ⁡(s∈S^T∗)=1−(1−ps)T.\mathbb{P}\left(s\in\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}\right)=1-(1-p_{s})^{T}~. (11)
Theorem 1 (Recovery in probability of the qq-observable structure set).

For every s∈S∗s\in S^{\ast},

limT→∞ℙ⁡(s∈S^T∗)={1,cs≤q,0,cs>q.\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{P}\left(s\in\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}\right)=\begin{cases}1,&c_{s}\leq q,\\ 0,&c_{s}>q.\end{cases}

Consequently, with

Sq∗={s∈S∗:cs≤q},S_{q}^{\ast}=\{s\in S^{\ast}:c_{s}\leq q\}~,

we have ℙ⁡(S^T∗=Sq∗)→1\mathbb{P}(\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}=S_{q}^{\ast})\rightarrow 1. In particular, if q≥maxs∈S∗⁡cs\displaystyle q\geq\max_{s\in S^{\ast}}c_{s}, then ℙ⁡(S^T∗=S∗)→1\mathbb{P}(\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}=S^{\ast})\rightarrow 1.

Proof.

If cs>qc_{s}>q, then Lemma 1 gives ps=0p_{s}=0, and Eq. (11) gives ℙ⁡(s∈S^T∗)=0\mathbb{P}(s\in\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast})=0 for all TT. If cs≤qc_{s}\leq q, then ps>0p_{s}>0, so (1−ps)T→0(1-p_{s})^{T}\rightarrow 0 and Eq. (11) gives ℙ⁡(s∈S^T∗)→1\mathbb{P}(s\in\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast})\rightarrow 1.

Structures in S∗∖Sq∗S^{\ast}\setminus S_{q}^{\ast} are never observed with qq clusters per mini-batch. Thus, S^T∗⊆Sq∗\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}\subseteq S_{q}^{\ast} for every TT. Since Sq∗S_{q}^{\ast} is finite, the union bound gives

ℙ(S^T∗≠Sq∗)=ℙ(⋃s∈Sq∗{s∉S^T∗})≤∑s∈Sq∗ℙ(s∉S^T∗)=∑s∈Sq∗(1−ps)T.\mathbb{P}\left(\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}\neq S_{q}^{\ast}\right)=\mathbb{P}\big(\bigcup_{s\in S_{q}^{\ast}}\{s\notin\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}\}\big)\leq\sum_{s\in S_{q}^{\ast}}\mathbb{P}\left(s\notin\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}\right)=\sum_{s\in S_{q}^{\ast}}(1-p_{s})^{T}~.

The right-hand side tends to zero as T→∞T\rightarrow\infty, so ℙ⁡(S^T∗=Sq∗)→1\mathbb{P}(\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}=S_{q}^{\ast})\rightarrow 1. If q≥maxs∈S∗⁡cs\displaystyle q\geq\max_{s\in S^{\ast}}c_{s}, then Sq∗=S∗S_{q}^{\ast}=S^{\ast}, which gives the full-recovery claim. ∎

C.5 Structural coverage convergence

We now aggregate the per-structure recovery probabilities into a global coverage quantity. The realized structural coverage after TT epochs is the random variable

Rq,T=|S^T∗||S∗|=1|S∗|∑s∈Sq∗𝟏{s∈S^T∗}.R_{q,T}=\frac{\left|\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}\right|}{\left|S^{\ast}\right|}=\frac{1}{\left|S^{\ast}\right|}\sum_{s\in S_{q}^{\ast}}\mathbf{1}\{s\in\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}\}~. (12)

Thus, Rq,TR_{q,T} is the fraction of global structures recovered by epoch TT. Its expectation defines the corresponding deterministic coverage curve. By linearity of expectation and Eq. (11),

𝔼⁡[Rq,T]=1|S∗|​∑s∈Sq∗ℙ⁡(s∈S^T∗)=1|S∗|​∑s∈Sq∗(1−(1−ps)T).\mathbb{E}[R_{q,T}]=\frac{1}{\left|S^{\ast}\right|}\sum_{s\in S_{q}^{\ast}}\mathbb{P}\left(s\in\widehat{S}_{T}^{\ast}\right)=\frac{1}{\left|S^{\ast}\right|}\sum_{s\in S_{q}^{\ast}}\left(1-\left(1-p_{s}\right)^{T}\right)~. (13)
Proposition 2 (Expected structural coverage convergence).

We have

limT→∞𝔼⁡[Rq,T]=|Sq∗||S∗|.\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}[R_{q,T}]=\frac{\left|S_{q}^{\ast}\right|}{\left|S^{\ast}\right|}~.

In particular, if q≥maxs∈S∗⁡cs\displaystyle q\geq\max_{s\in S^{\ast}}c_{s}, then limT→∞𝔼⁡[Rq,T]=1\displaystyle\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}[R_{q,T}]=1.

Proof.

Since S∗S^{\ast} is finite, we can pass the limit through the finite sum in Eq. (13):

limT→∞𝔼⁡[Rq,T]=1|S∗|​∑s∈Sq∗limT→∞(1−(1−ps)T).\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}[R_{q,T}]=\frac{1}{\left|S^{\ast}\right|}\sum_{s\in S_{q}^{\ast}}\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}\left(1-\left(1-p_{s}\right)^{T}\right)~.

For s∈Sq∗s\in S_{q}^{\ast}, Lemma 1 gives ps>0p_{s}>0, so the corresponding limit is 11. Therefore,

limT→∞𝔼⁡[Rq,T]=1|S∗|​∑s∈Sq∗1=|Sq∗||S∗|.\lim_{T\rightarrow\infty}\mathbb{E}[R_{q,T}]=\frac{1}{\left|S^{\ast}\right|}\sum_{s\in S_{q}^{\ast}}1=\frac{\left|S_{q}^{\ast}\right|}{\left|S^{\ast}\right|}~.

If q≥maxs∈S∗⁡cs\displaystyle q\geq\max_{s\in S^{\ast}}c_{s}, then Sq∗=S∗S_{q}^{\ast}=S^{\ast}, which gives the full-coverage claim. ∎

C.6 Repeated-exposure structural coverage

One-exposure coverage does not distinguish structures observed once from those observed repeatedly. For a threshold m∈{1,…,T}m\in\{1,\ldots,T\}, define the realized mm-exposure structural coverage as

Rq,T(m)=1|S∗|∑s∈S∗𝟏{Ns(T)≥m}=1|S∗|∑s∈Sq∗𝟏{Ns(T)≥m}.R_{q,T}^{(m)}=\frac{1}{|S^{\ast}|}\sum_{s\in S^{\ast}}\mathbf{1}\{N_{s}(T)\geq m\}=\frac{1}{|S^{\ast}|}\sum_{s\in S_{q}^{\ast}}\mathbf{1}\{N_{s}(T)\geq m\}~. (14)

The second equality follows because Ns​(T)=0N_{s}(T)=0 almost surely for s∉Sq∗s\notin S_{q}^{\ast}. Moreover,

Rq,T(1)=Rq,T,R_{q,T}^{(1)}=R_{q,T}, (15)

Thus, cumulative structural coverage is the case m=1m=1.

Proposition 3 (Expected repeated-exposure coverage).

For every m∈{1,…,T}m\in\{1,\ldots,T\},

𝔼⁡[Rq,T(m)]=1|S∗|​∑s∈Sq∗[1−∑j=0m−1(Tj)​psj​(1−ps)T−j].\mathbb{E}\left[R_{q,T}^{(m)}\right]=\frac{1}{|S^{\ast}|}\sum_{s\in S_{q}^{\ast}}\left[1-\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\binom{T}{j}p_{s}^{j}(1-p_{s})^{T-j}\right]~. (16)
Proof.

By linearity of expectation,

𝔼⁡[Rq,T(m)]=1|S∗|​∑s∈Sq∗ℙ⁡(Ns​(T)≥m).\mathbb{E}\left[R_{q,T}^{(m)}\right]=\frac{1}{|S^{\ast}|}\sum_{s\in S_{q}^{\ast}}\mathbb{P}\left(N_{s}(T)\geq m\right).

Proposition 1 gives Ns​(T)∼Binomial⁡(T,ps)N_{s}(T)\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(T,p_{s}). Complementing the events Ns​(T)=jN_{s}(T)=j for j∈{0,…,m−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\} gives Eq. (16). Independence between different structures is not required. ∎

For a fixed partition, define the cluster-span counts and span-specific recovery probabilities as

nc=|{s∈S∗:cs=c}|,pc​(q)={(q−1c−1)(K−1c−1),c≤q,0,c>q.n_{c}=\left|\{s\in S^{\ast}:c_{s}=c\}\right|,\qquad p_{c}(q)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\binom{q-1}{c-1}}{\binom{K-1}{c-1}},&c\leq q,\\[11.00008pt] 0,&c>q.\end{cases} (17)

Since ps=pcs​(q)p_{s}=p_{c_{s}}(q), grouping Eq. (16) by cluster span gives

𝔼⁡[Rq,T(m)]=1|S∗|​∑c=1qnc​[1−∑j=0m−1(Tj)​pc​(q)j​(1−pc​(q))T−j].\mathbb{E}\left[R_{q,T}^{(m)}\right]=\frac{1}{|S^{\ast}|}\sum_{c=1}^{q}n_{c}\left[1-\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\binom{T}{j}p_{c}(q)^{j}\left(1-p_{c}(q)\right)^{T-j}\right]~. (18)

For m=1m=1, Eq. (18) reduces to the expected cumulative coverage in Eq. (13).

Corollary 1 (Fixed-threshold coverage convergence).

For every fixed m≥1m\geq 1,

Rq,T(m)⟶|Sq∗||S∗|almost surely as ​T→∞.R_{q,T}^{(m)}\longrightarrow\frac{|S_{q}^{\ast}|}{|S^{\ast}|}\qquad\text{almost surely as }T\to\infty. (19)

Consequently,

limT→∞𝔼⁡[Rq,T(m)]=|Sq∗||S∗|.\lim_{T\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[R_{q,T}^{(m)}\right]=\frac{|S_{q}^{\ast}|}{|S^{\ast}|}~.
Proof.

Every s∈Sq∗s\in S_{q}^{\ast} has ps>0p_{s}>0. Eq. (9) therefore implies Ns​(T)→∞N_{s}(T)\to\infty almost surely. Hence, 𝟏{Ns(T)≥m}→1\mathbf{1}\{N_{s}(T)\geq m\}\to 1 almost surely for each fixed mm. Structures outside Sq∗S_{q}^{\ast} have zero exposure, and Sq∗S_{q}^{\ast} is finite. Eq. (14) then gives the almost-sure limit. Bounded convergence gives the corresponding expectation because 0≤Rq,T(m)≤10\leq R_{q,T}^{(m)}\leq 1. ∎

At finite TT, exposure differs across cluster spans because the expected count is T​pc​(q)Tp_{c}(q).

C.7 Mean structural exposure rate

Thresholded coverage discards differences beyond its prescribed number of exposures. We therefore define the realized mean structural exposure rate as

Φq,T=1|S∗|​∑s∈S∗Ns​(T)T.\Phi_{q,T}=\frac{1}{|S^{\ast}|}\sum_{s\in S^{\ast}}\frac{N_{s}(T)}{T}~. (20)

Equivalently, Φq,T\Phi_{q,T} is the fraction of structure-epoch pairs in which the corresponding global structure is available.

Proposition 4 (Mean structural exposure rate).

For every T≥1T\geq 1,

𝔼⁡[Φq,T]=Φq:=1|S∗|​∑s∈S∗ps=1|S∗|​∑c=1qnc​pc​(q).\mathbb{E}[\Phi_{q,T}]=\Phi_{q}:=\frac{1}{|S^{\ast}|}\sum_{s\in S^{\ast}}p_{s}=\frac{1}{|S^{\ast}|}\sum_{c=1}^{q}n_{c}p_{c}(q)~. (21)

Moreover,

Φq,T⟶Φqalmost surely as ​T→∞.\Phi_{q,T}\longrightarrow\Phi_{q}\qquad\text{almost surely as }T\to\infty. (22)
Proof.

Eq. (8) gives 𝔼⁡[Ns​(T)/T]=ps\mathbb{E}[N_{s}(T)/T]=p_{s}. Linearity of expectation and grouping by cluster span give Eq. (21). For each s∈S∗s\in S^{\ast}, Eq. (9) gives Ns​(T)/T→psN_{s}(T)/T\to p_{s} almost surely. Averaging over the finite set S∗S^{\ast} gives Eq. (22). ∎

Unlike fixed-threshold coverage, Φq\Phi_{q} retains span-dependent exposure imbalance as thresholded coverage approaches its limit. Since each epoch contains MM optimization steps, the corresponding average frequency among training steps is

1|S∗|​∑s∈S∗Ns​(T)M​T=Φq,TM⟶ΦqMalmost surely.\frac{1}{|S^{\ast}|}\sum_{s\in S^{\ast}}\frac{N_{s}(T)}{MT}=\frac{\Phi_{q,T}}{M}\longrightarrow\frac{\Phi_{q}}{M}\qquad\text{almost surely}. (23)

These quantities alone describe structural availability. They do not determine optimization behavior or predictive performance.

C.8 Exposure epoch distribution

The exposure count also identifies when a structure accumulates a prescribed number of exposures. For m≥1m\geq 1, define the epoch of the mm-th exposure as

Ts(m)=inf{t∈ℕ:Ns​(t)≥m},T_{s}^{(m)}=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{N}:N_{s}(t)\geq m\}, (24)

with the convention that the infimum of the empty set is ∞\infty.

Proposition 5 (Epoch of the mm-th structural exposure).

If 0<ps<10<p_{s}<1, then Ts(m)T_{s}^{(m)} follows the negative-binomial distribution

ℙ(Ts(m)=ℓ)=(ℓ−1m−1)psm(1−ps)ℓ−m,ℓ=m,m+1,….\mathbb{P}\left(T_{s}^{(m)}=\ell\right)=\binom{\ell-1}{m-1}p_{s}^{m}(1-p_{s})^{\ell-m},\qquad\ell=m,m+1,\ldots. (25)

If ps=1p_{s}=1, then Ts(m)=mT_{s}^{(m)}=m almost surely. For every ps>0p_{s}>0, its expectation and variance are

𝔼⁡[Ts(m)]=mps,Var⁡[Ts(m)]=m⁡(1−ps)ps2.\mathbb{E}\left[T_{s}^{(m)}\right]=\frac{m}{p_{s}},\qquad\operatorname{Var}\left[T_{s}^{(m)}\right]=\frac{m(1-p_{s})}{p_{s}^{2}}~. (26)

If ps=0p_{s}=0, then Ts(m)=∞T_{s}^{(m)}=\infty almost surely.

Proof.

Let Xs(t)=𝟏{s∈S(t)}X_{s}^{(t)}=\mathbf{1}\{s\in S^{(t)}\} denote the exposure indicator of structure ss at epoch tt, which forms an i.i.d. sequence of Bernoulli⁡(ps)\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_{s}) random variables. Let Ns​(t)=∑i=1tXs(i)N_{s}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{t}X_{s}^{(i)} be the cumulative exposure count up to epoch tt.

Case 1: 0<ps<10<p_{s}<1.

{Ts(m)=ℓ}={Ns(ℓ−1)=m−1}∩{Xs(ℓ)=1}.\{T_{s}^{(m)}=\ell\}=\{N_{s}(\ell-1)=m-1\}\cap\{X_{s}^{(\ell)}=1\}.

ℙ⁡(Ts(m)=ℓ)\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\left(T_{s}^{(m)}=\ell\right) =ℙ⁡(Ns​(ℓ−1)=m−1)⋅ℙ⁡(Xs(ℓ)=1)\displaystyle=\mathbb{P}\left(N_{s}(\ell-1)=m-1\right)\cdot\mathbb{P}\left(X_{s}^{(\ell)}=1\right)
=[(ℓ−1m−1)​psm−1​(1−ps)(ℓ−1)−(m−1)]⋅ps\displaystyle=\left[\binom{\ell-1}{m-1}p_{s}^{m-1}(1-p_{s})^{(\ell-1)-(m-1)}\right]\cdot p_{s}
=(ℓ−1m−1)psm(1−ps)ℓ−m,ℓ=m,m+1,…,\displaystyle=\binom{\ell-1}{m-1}p_{s}^{m}(1-p_{s})^{\ell-m},\qquad\ell=m,m+1,\ldots,

which establishes Eq. (25).

To derive the moments in Eq. (26), we represent Ts(m)T_{s}^{(m)} as the sum of mm inter-arrival waiting times:

𝔼⁡[Wk]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[W_{k}] =∑w=1∞w​(1−ps)w−1​ps=ps​∑w=1∞w​p¯sw−1\displaystyle=\sum_{w=1}^{\infty}w(1-p_{s})^{w-1}p_{s}=p_{s}\sum_{w=1}^{\infty}w\overline{p}_{s}^{w-1}
=ps​dd​p¯s​(∑w=0∞p¯sw)=ps​dd​p¯s​(11−p¯s)=ps⋅1(1−p¯s)2=psps2=1ps.\displaystyle=p_{s}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\overline{p}_{s}}\left(\sum_{w=0}^{\infty}\overline{p}_{s}^{w}\right)=p_{s}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\overline{p}_{s}}\left(\frac{1}{1-\overline{p}_{s}}\right)=p_{s}\cdot\frac{1}{(1-\overline{p}_{s})^{2}}=\frac{p_{s}}{p_{s}^{2}}=\frac{1}{p_{s}}.

𝔼⁡[Ts(m)]=∑k=1m𝔼⁡[Wk]=∑k=1m1ps=mps.\mathbb{E}\left[T_{s}^{(m)}\right]=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}[W_{k}]=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{1}{p_{s}}=\frac{m}{p_{s}}.

Second, for the variance of the finite sum, we expand:

Var⁡[Ts(m)]=∑k=1mVar⁡(Wk)+∑1≤i<j≤mCov⁡(Wi,Wj).\operatorname{Var}\left[T_{s}^{(m)}\right]=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\operatorname{Var}(W_{k})+2\!\!\!\!\!\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq m}\!\!\!\!\!\operatorname{Cov}(W_{i},W_{j}).

=ps​p¯s​d2d​p¯s2​(11−p¯s)=ps​p¯s⋅2(1−p¯s)3=2​ps​(1−ps)ps3=2​(1−ps)ps2.\displaystyle=p_{s}\overline{p}_{s}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{2}}{\mathrm{d}\overline{p}_{s}^{2}}\left(\frac{1}{1-\overline{p}_{s}}\right)=p_{s}\overline{p}_{s}\cdot\frac{2}{(1-\overline{p}_{s})^{3}}=\frac{2p_{s}(1-p_{s})}{p_{s}^{3}}=\frac{2(1-p_{s})}{p_{s}^{2}}.

Var⁡[Ts(m)]=∑k=1mVar⁡(Wk)=∑k=1m1−psps2=m⁡(1−ps)ps2.\operatorname{Var}\left[T_{s}^{(m)}\right]=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\operatorname{Var}(W_{k})=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{1-p_{s}}{p_{s}^{2}}=\frac{m(1-p_{s})}{p_{s}^{2}}.
Case 2: ps=1p_{s}=1.

If ps=1p_{s}=1, then Xs(t)=1X_{s}^{(t)}=1 almost surely for all t∈ℕt\in\mathbb{N}, so Ns​(t)=tN_{s}(t)=t almost surely. The stopping condition Ns​(t)≥mN_{s}(t)\geq m simplifies to t≥mt\geq m, yielding Ts(m)=mT_{s}^{(m)}=m almost surely. Substituting ps=1p_{s}=1 into Eq. (26) confirms 𝔼⁡[Ts(m)]=m\mathbb{E}\left[T_{s}^{(m)}\right]=m and Var⁡[Ts(m)]=0\operatorname{Var}\left[T_{s}^{(m)}\right]=0.
